outcome: Since 26 January 2024 one event bears directly on the game: Cain, Raymond and Källersjö's computer-assisted proof (arXiv:2509.21494, 25 Sep 2025) that the first player has no winning strategy on the 7x7x7 board, so the least winning dimension for width 7 is at least 4; widths 5 and 6 at dimension 3 remain open and no width's exact value changed. The 2026 Hales-Jewett preprints (Mouhib; Conlon, Farnsworth and Robertson; Shelah) concern 2-colouring numbers, a different quantity, and are recorded as such.
problem_asks: (1) For each width n (side length of the board), the least dimension d(n) such that the first player X has a winning strategy in the n-dimensional tic-tac-toe game on [n]^d, where a win is completing a line of n cells (combinatorial lines, as in the Hales-Jewett setting). (2) The exact value of d(n) as a function of n, which the question's phrase 'what is the smallest dimension' asks for. (3) The guarantee is a winning strategy for X specifically, not a draw; the cross-reference to the Hales-Jewett theorem and the nd game is context, not a further part. The question does not ask for the Hales-Jewett numbers themselves, nor for the r-player version.

events.what_happened: Hales and Jewett, 'Regularity and positional games' (Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 106 (1963), pp. 222-229), proved the Hales-Jewett theorem and the n^d game results: the second player cannot win (strategy stealing), and for each width there is a dimension beyond which the first player wins. MathWorld and the 2026 survey cite it for these results. I did not open the original paper.
events.delivers: Existence only. For each width n there is some dimension at which X has a winning strategy, and O never does. No value of d(n) is given, and the dimension the argument yields is far larger than any computed value.
events.remains: The exact value of d(n) at every width, and the first-player outcome at every width and dimension below the existence bound.

checked_by.who: Transactions of the American Mathematical Society (journal of record)
checked_by.qualification: refereed research journal; the venue is known from citations, the refereeing itself was not checked
checked_by.what_they_did: published the paper (known from citations only)

events.direction: Existence result that cuts toward a first-player win at large enough dimension, which is the direction the question points.

events.what_happened: Erdos and Selfridge, 'On a combinatorial game' (J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 14 (1973)). Per search excerpts, it gives an explicit drawing strategy for the second player in positional games, applied to n-dimensional tic-tac-toe as an improvement on a Hales-Jewett drawing result, and states the Erdos-Selfridge criterion. The PDF at users.renyi.hu returned only excerpts to me; I did not read the paper.
events.delivers: By the Erdos-Selfridge criterion as cited (second player wins as Breaker if the sum over winning sets W of 2^(-|W|) is below 1/2), for each fixed dimension d the second player can force a draw once the width n is large, so X has no winning strategy in that dimension for large n. This gives d(n) tending to infinity, with no value of d(n) and no explicit threshold.
events.remains: Exact d(n) at every width; the threshold width beyond which each dimension is drawn.

checked_by.who: Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A (journal of record)
checked_by.qualification: refereed research journal; refereeing not checked
checked_by.what_they_did: published the paper (known from citations only)

events.doubts: The reading of the criterion as giving a threshold for each dimension is my own arithmetic on the cited sum, not a statement I read in the paper. Some secondary summaries state the bound as 2^n rather than 2^(n-1), so the constant is unverified.
events.direction: Draw for the second player at large width relative to the dimension, which cuts against an X win there.

events.what_happened: Golomb and Hales, 'Hypercube Tic-Tac-Toe', in More Games of No Chance (MSRI Publications 42, 2002). From secondary sources: they conjecture, for each dimension k, a critical width below which the first player wins and at or above which the second player can draw (the pairing threshold is at least as large); they note that the 2^k board is a first-player win on the second move; and they give an explicit Breaker pairing strategy on the 8x8x8 board, which the 2025 cubic paper cites as their result [8]. The SLMath PDF returned binary to me, so I did not read the paper.
events.delivers: Width 8 at dimension 3: a second-player draw under standard rules (as cited by the 2025 paper), so d(8) is at least 4. Otherwise conjectural critical widths n_k with no exact values for d(n).
events.remains: The conjectured thresholds for every dimension; exact d(n) at every width.
events.doubts: The n_k thresholds are conjectures in the paper as described; the width 8 draw is cited to them by a 2025 paper and by MathWorld (which attributes it to Golomb via Ma 2005), and I did not read the original argument.
events.direction: Second-player draws at large width, cutting against an X win at those widths and dimensions.

events.what_happened: Eugene Mahalko, 'A Possible Win Strategy for the Game of Qubic', M.Sc. thesis, Brigham Young University, 1976, as cited in Wikipedia's 3D tic-tac-toe article, which describes it as a weak solution: under optimal play the first player wins 4x4x4. I found no library record or full text.
events.delivers: Existence of a first-player win at width 4, dimension 3, under optimal play, with no strategy given. Says nothing about dimension 2.
events.remains: Width 4 at dimension 2 (not addressed); all other widths.
events.doubts: Known only from a Wikipedia summary and citation. The later solutions by Patashnik and Allis supersede it, so no independent check of the thesis itself is on record in my sources.
events.direction: First-player win at width 4, dimension 3, the direction the question's guarantee asks for.
events.object: Existence claim only (weak solution): the first player wins 4x4x4 with optimal play. No strategy is described in the sources I read.

events.what_happened: Oren Patashnik, 'Qubic: 4x4x4 Tic-Tac-Toe', Mathematics Magazine 53(4), September 1980. Per Wikipedia and the 2025 cubic paper, a computer-assisted proof, using pruned game-tree search with isomorphism pruning, that the first player wins 4x4x4 under perfect play, with a complete first-player winning strategy and about 1500 hours of computer time. The ranger.uta.edu PDF returned binary to me, so the paper text was not read; the details come from Wikipedia, the 2025 cubic paper (which cites it as [2]) and search excerpts.
events.delivers: Width 4 at dimension 3: the first player has a winning strategy under perfect play, so d(4) is at most 3. With a second-player draw at width 4 in dimension 2 (Uiterwijk 2017, separate event), d(4) = 3 if that draw is right.
events.remains: d(n) at every width other than 4 (and the dimension-2 value at width 4 is covered by the separate Uiterwijk event).

checked_by.who: Ken Thompson (per a December 2025 post on the TUHS mailing list, recounting the 1980 check)
checked_by.qualification: computer scientist, asked by Elwyn Berlekamp to verify the solution when it was submitted
checked_by.what_they_did: reports (retrospectively, 2025) that he verified the solution at Berlekamp's request and that it was a win
checked_by.where: https://www.tuhs.org/pipermail/tuhs/2025-December/032895.html (seen in a search excerpt; not opened)

events.doubts: The complete-strategy claim rests on Wikipedia's summary and the paper's own text, which I could not read. Thompson's account is a 2025 recollection. A Rochester course page says the result was not known until the early 1990s, which conflicts with 1980 and which I treat as an error (see disputes).
events.direction: First-player win at width 4, dimension 3, the direction the question's guarantee asks for.
events.object: A complete first-player winning strategy for 4x4x4 (Qubic), presented as a computer-generated game tree according to Wikipedia. It is an explicit winning strategy, constructive in principle, but too large to reproduce by hand.

ai.disclosed_cost: about 1500 hours of computer time, per Wikipedia

events.what_happened: L. V. Allis and P. N. A. Schoo, 'Qubic solved again' (year 1992 in the citation given in Wikipedia's 3D article). An independent solution of 4x4x4 Qubic showing the first-player win, using proof-number search, a game-tree search method Allis devised. Other sources date it to 1991 (a Darse Billings note) or 1994 (NBC News). I did not open the paper and could not confirm its venue.
events.delivers: Second, independent confirmation that the first player wins at width 4, dimension 3 (so d(4) is at most 3). No new width or dimension.
events.remains: Same as Patashnik 1980: d(n) at every width other than 4.
events.doubts: The year is disputed across sources (1991, 1992, 1994); I give 1992 from the citation.

events.what_happened: Mikhail Lavrov, 'An upper bound for the Hales-Jewett number HJ(4,2)' (arXiv:1504.02753, submitted 10 Apr 2015, one version). For n at least 10^11, every 2-colouring of [4]^n contains a monochromatic combinatorial line, so HJ(4,2) is at most 10^11, improving the Shelah-based bound of roughly 2 up-arrow-up-arrow 7 to 8.
events.delivers: A bound on the 2-colouring number HJ(4,2), not on the game. By my inference (not stated in the paper), an upper bound on HJ(n,2) gives d(n) at most HJ(n,2), so this gives d(4) at most 10^11, which the Patashnik result supersedes. It does not address the game.
events.direction: Coloring result: every 2-colouring of [4]^n has a line for n at least 10^11. Toward forced lines, which is a different question from a first-player win.

events.what_happened: N. Hindman and E. Tressler, 'The First Nontrivial Hales-Jewett Number is Four', Ars Combinatoria 113 (2014), 385-390: HJ(3,2) = 4, so every 2-colouring of [3]^4 has a monochromatic line and some 2-colouring of [3]^3 has none. Secondary sources (Lavrov 2015; the 2026 Conlon, Farnsworth and Robertson preprint) describe the proof as partly computer-assisted. I did not open the original.
events.delivers: A 2-colouring number, not the game. By my inference, d(3) is at most HJ(3,2) = 4. The existence of a line-free 2-colouring of [3]^3 does not contradict a first-player win at dimension 3, because a game play has a fixed split of cells between the players (alternating moves), and not every colouring is a play. The game value d(3) = 3 is established by other sources (Gardner 1979 via MathWorld; Wikipedia 3D article).
events.doubts: The computer-assisted part is described only in secondary sources; I did not see the computation.
events.direction: Colouring result: a line-free 2-colouring of [3]^3 exists. Not a game outcome.

events.what_happened: Jos Uiterwijk, 'Set Matching: An Enhancement of the Hales-Jewett Pairing Strategy' (arXiv:1703.10678, submitted 16 Mar 2017). The abstract states 'the direct proof (without further investigation) that the empty 4 x 4 board is a draw for 4-in-a-Row', using a set-matching pairing strategy. I read only the abstract; the body and any journal publication were not checked.
events.revisions: v1 seen; no later version seen
events.delivers: The two-dimensional 4x4 board with four-in-a-row (width 4, dimension 2): a second-player draw, so X has no winning strategy there, which gives d(4) at least 3. This is the only source I found that proves the 4x4 two-dimensional draw directly. It is a single abstract-level claim.
events.remains: d(n) at every width other than 4 (and the width-4 value is only as strong as this claim plus the Patashnik result).
events.directly_checkable: The pairing for the 4x4 board is a finite certificate a reader could check by hand; I did not do so.
events.doubts: Single author, abstract-level read; no independent corroboration. MathWorld gives a 5x5 draw for four-in-a-row but no 4x4 statement; the 2026 survey's general claim that m=n=k>=3 boards are draws (see disputes) would cover 4x4 but its source is unidentified and conflicts with MathWorld on widths 6 and 7.
events.direction: Second-player draw at width 4 in dimension 2, which cuts against an X win there.
events.object: The pairing strategy of the set-matching method, applied to the 4x4 board with four-in-a-row, giving a draw. Constructive, as far as the abstract says.

events.what_happened: Luca Bastioni, Alessandro Giannoni and Javier Lobillo-Olmedo, 'Thresholds for Tic-Tac-Toe on Finite Affine Spaces' (arXiv:2605.05455, v1 6 May 2026, v3 22 May 2026). Affine tic-tac-toe on F_q^m, where the first player to occupy all points of an n-dimensional affine subspace wins; each game is a first-player win or a draw, monotone in m, giving a threshold T(n,q); they show T(1,q) = 2 for q in {2,3,4}, T(2,2) = 4, and T(n,2) at most 2^(n+1).
events.revisions: v1 6 May 2026; v2 8 May 2026; v3 22 May 2026 (current)
events.delivers: A different game: affine subspaces of finite spaces over F_q, not n-in-a-row on [n]^d. Its threshold is structurally the same kind of quantity as d(n), but it bears on the cube game only by analogy, and the paper does not mention Hales-Jewett or the cube.
events.remains: The question as asked, which concerns [n]^d.
events.direction: Not about the cube game; recorded as a discounted neighbouring result.

events.what_happened: John W. Cain, Ioannis M. Raymond and Nora C. Källersjö, 'Cubic tic-tac-toe: A matching-based approach' (arXiv:2509.21494, math.CO, v1 only, 21 pages). The paper proves, under Maker-Breaker rules, that Breaker has a winning strategy in the 7x7x7 game (Theorem 4.1), and states (Corollary 4.2) that under standard rules either player can force a draw. So X has no winning strategy on width 7, dimension 3. The method is computer-assisted: O's first four moves (or three, depending on X's opening) are fixed so that the remaining play follows a pairing found as a maximal matching in a bipartite graph, computed with Hopcroft-Karp. It checks 22,163,142 configurations after an opening at the centre (matchings of size 332 over 166 surviving lines) and 12,824,370 otherwise (matchings of size 336 over 168 lines). The introduction states the known results: the first player wins for n at most 4 (citing Patashnik), either player forces a draw for n at least 8 (citing Golomb and Hales), and widths 5 and 6 are open.
events.revisions: v1 25 Sep 2025 only; no later version listed on the abstract page when fetched
events.delivers: Width 7 at dimension 3 only: no first-player winning strategy under standard rules, so d(7) is at least 4. It establishes nothing about widths 5 and 6 at dimension 3, nothing about whether X wins at width 7 in dimension 4 or above, and nothing about any other width. It is a restricted case of the question: one width, one dimension, and the claim is a negative one about X.
events.remains: Width 5 and width 6 at dimension 3 (open per the paper). Width 7 at every dimension of 4 or more, so d(7) is known only to be at least 4. Widths 5 and 6 at dimension 2 are not addressed by this paper (see the survey and MathWorld for claims there).
events.directly_checkable: The proof is a finite computation whose output is explicit: for each listed configuration, a perfect matching of the stated size gives Breaker's answers. The authors say their code and compilation instructions are at people.math.harvard.edu/~jcain2/tic-tac-toe-code.tar.gz (linked from the arXiv HTML). I did not download or run it.
events.doubts: No public check found. It is unrefereed (no journal reference), computer-assisted, and the code had not been re-run by anyone I could find. The paper's statements about widths 4 and at least 8 are cited to Patashnik and Golomb-Hales in the body, which I read only in part. No specific error has been identified.
events.direction: Cuts against a first-player win at width 7 in dimension 3, so the least winning dimension for width 7 exceeds 3.
events.object: A computer-verified pairing strategy for the second player on the 7x7x7 board: after four opening moves for each side (three if X does not open at the centre), the surviving lines admit a perfect matching (size 332 or 336) that tells O how to answer, and the paper checks all such configurations. It shows that X cannot force a win in dimension 3 at width 7. It is explicit as a finite certificate, not a non-constructive existence argument.

ai.disclosed_cost: about five hours of computation on the first author's laptop, per the paper

events.what_happened: Younes Mouhib, arXiv:2606.22155, v1 20 Jun 2026 and v2 24 Jul 2026. The abstract page (v2, single author, title 'Lower Bounds for the Hales-Jewett Numbers via Symmetric and One-Weight Colorings') states HJ(3,3) at least 22 and HJ(4,2) at least 14, improving the previous records 14 and 12. HJ(t,r) is the least d such that every r-colouring of [t]^d has a monochromatic combinatorial line. The method identifies symmetric colourings with one-weight colourings and optimises the weight. Per search excerpts, v1 was co-authored with Lorenz Halbeisen and titled 'Improved Lower Bounds for the Hales-Jewett Numbers via Symmetric Colorings'; I did not open v1 directly. v2 says it supersedes v1 and arXiv:2607.02226.
events.revisions: v1 20 Jun 2026 (per search excerpt: Mouhib and Halbeisen, 'Improved Lower Bounds ... via Symmetric Colorings'); v2 24 Jul 2026 (single author, 'consolidated and substantially expanded', supersedes v1 and 2607.02226)
events.delivers: Lower bounds on two 2-colouring-type numbers: HJ(3,3) at least 22 (three letters, three colours) and HJ(4,2) at least 14 (four letters, two colours). These say a line-free colouring exists in dimension 21 and dimension 13 respectively. They are not about the first-player game. A lower bound on HJ(n,2) gives no lower bound on d(n), because a line-free colouring is necessary for a draw but the converse fails, so these results do not move the question.
events.remains: The whole game question. For the colouring numbers, HJ(3,3) and HJ(4,2) remain undetermined.
events.directly_checkable: Certificates are explicit colourings: a palette deciding all 4,387,586,157,901 lines of [3]^21 with 253 coloured cells for the 22 bound, and a 26-periodic palette deciding all 1,153,594,261 lines of [4]^13 for the 14 bound. The abstract says each displayed certificate is verified by direct enumeration; the scripts are at github.com/ysmouhib/hj-certificates (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21537624). Not run by me.
events.doubts: Author-stated results. The v2 text says some forcing (upper-bound) claims rest on SAT solvers, which the lower-bound certificates do not need. The authorship changed between versions (see disputes). No substantive doubt found.
events.direction: Lower bounds on colouring numbers: more line-free colourings exist than previously known. This cuts toward avoiding lines, a different question from who wins the game.
events.object: Explicit line-free 2-colourings and 3-colourings given as palettes (the 22 bound uses weight (0,1,29) and 253 coloured cells on [3]^21; the 14 bound uses weight (0,2,3,5) and a period-26 palette on [4]^13). Constructive; each is checkable by enumeration of lines.
people: Lorenz Halbeisen (co-author on v1 per search excerpt; not named in v2)

events.what_happened: Younes Mouhib, 'One-Weight Colorings, the Symmetric Class, and Lower Bounds for Hales-Jewett Numbers' (arXiv:2607.02226, v1 2 Jul 2026, single author, ETH Zurich affiliation on the paper). Same bounds: HJ(3,3) at least 22 (Theorem 5.1, marked computer-assisted, weight (0,1,29), 253 cells) and HJ(4,2) at least 14 (Theorem 5.5, marked computer-verified, weight (0,2,3,5), period-26 palette), with the claim that every displayed certificate was re-verified by direct enumeration. It also reports a census: of 1644 line-free 2-colourings of [3]^3, 36 are symmetric. A footnote says the note extracts material from the author's MSc thesis under the supervision of L. Halbeisen, and reference [28] is 'Mouhib and Halbeisen (2026)'.
events.revisions: v1 2 Jul 2026 only (as fetched); superseded per 2606.22155 v2
events.delivers: The same colouring-number lower bounds as the 2606.22155 event, with a census of line-free 2-colourings of [3]^3. Not about the first-player game, and it does not move d(n) for the reasons given in the 2606.22155 event.
events.directly_checkable: An ancillary file (anc/verify.py) is said by the paper to re-derive every displayed certificate by enumeration. I did not run it.
events.direction: Lower bounds on colouring numbers, as for 2606.22155; not a game outcome.
events.object: The same explicit palettes as 2606.22155 (weight (0,1,29) on [3]^21 with 253 cells; weight (0,2,3,5) with a period-26 palette on [4]^13). Constructive.

events.what_happened: Nathan Conlon, Nayda Farnsworth and Aaron Robertson, 'On Hales-Jewett and Related Numbers' (arXiv:2607.18111, math.CO, v1 only, submitted 20 Jul 2026, CC BY 4.0). Theorem 8 gives HJ(3;3) at least 14 by extending a van der Waerden colouring of [3]^12 to a colouring of [3]^13 with a SAT instance solved by CryptoMiniSat, reported as 8831 CPU hours over 15 cores. Remark 9 says that while writing, the authors learned that Mouhib and Halbeisen had proved HJ(3;3) at least 22. The paper also treats variants (off-diagonal, combinatorial-geometric, Connect Four number). It states, for the game, that 3x3x3 tic-tac-toe with 2 players always has a winner, citing Beck's book as an exercise; that is a restatement of a known fact. It also shows that Connect Four on a 5-dimensional hypercube of any side length can end in a draw, and it discusses 3-player tic-tac-toe.
events.delivers: On the colouring numbers: HJ(3;3) at least 14 by a SAT computation. On the game: nothing new about d(n). The 3x3x3 no-draw restatement agrees with d(3) = 3 but adds no new argument. The Connect Four and 3-player results are on different games and are discounted. So this event does not move the question.
events.doubts: The 8831 CPU-hour figure is from the HTML version; the search excerpt's count of nine satisfying colourings I did not confirm in the full text.
events.direction: Lower bound on a colouring number, plus discounted game variants. Not a result on the first-player game.
events.object: A van der Waerden-based colouring of [3]^12 extended by a SAT-found completion to [3]^13 with no monochromatic line (existence of a line-free colouring, explicit, found by computation).

ai.disclosed_cost: 8831 CPU hours over 15 cores (CryptoMiniSat), per the HTML version

events.what_happened: Saharon Shelah, 'HJ numbers revisited' (arXiv:2607.14732, report Sh:E117, math.CO). v1 16 Jul 2026, whose abstract (as shown on the abstract page) says the bounds on the Hales-Jewett numbers are improved to a tower of exponentiations, by improving the inductive step on alphabet size from towers to 2-exponentiations. v2 29 Sep 2026 (current) reads differently in its HTML text: it bounds the density Hales-Jewett numbers in the Grzegorczyk class E^5 (iterated tetration), says the earlier version's E^4 proof is retracted, and says a longer work will follow. The v2 abstract page describes the density version only as future work.
events.revisions: v1 16 Jul 2026; v2 29 Sep 2026 (current). The v2 text states the earlier version's proof is retracted and that the earlier claimed level was E^4; the text itself is inconsistent on E^4 versus E^5.
events.delivers: If the classical 2-colour numbers are the object (the v1 abstract's reading), this is an upper bound on HJ(n,2) of tower type. By my inference, that gives d(n) at most a tower function of n: a bound on the problem's quantity, though far from any value. If the object is the density number (the v2 reading), it bears on d(n) only through the classical implication, which the paper does not state. Either way it gives no exact value and no lower bound.
events.remains: The exact value of d(n) for every width.
events.doubts: The v2 text is internally inconsistent: E^4 in one place and E^5 in others; the abstract says the earlier proof is retracted; Conclusion 1.14 cites a 'Claim 2.2 of the full version' not in this typescript; and the arXiv abstract calls it a preliminary version with the main treatment deferred. No external reading found.

withdrawn.what: The earlier version's proof of an E^4 bound is described in the v2 text as retracted.

events.direction: Upper bound on a Hales-Jewett-type number; says nothing about lower bounds or exact values, and does not settle the game.

events.what_happened: Z. Adams, M. Z. Cassim, C. Hou, O. Knill, V. Seco Roopnaraine and M. H. Saleem, 'God numbers for Graphs, Games and Groups' (arXiv:2605.20243, math.HO, submitted 18 May 2026, 74 pages). A survey whose tic-tac-toe section (Section 10) lists the n^d game as background: Section 10.1 says 5x5x5 tic-tac-toe with 3^125 positions is unsolved (citing its reference [7]) and that (7,7,5) and (8,8,5) are computationally drawn (citing [35]); Section 10.4 states '(m,n,k) is a draw whenever m=n=k>=3' citing [7]; Section 10.6 says 'Qubic without gravity is a first-player win' citing [60]; Section 10.7 says 'For 3x3x3, there is always win' without a source. Section 4.4 says the 2x2 tic-tac-toe game 'has no draw. The initial player always wins. The god number is 2' (in the authors' framework; the win condition used there is not checked by me).
events.delivers: Not a new result on the question but a later source. It states the 2x2 case (width 2, dimension 2: first-player win, consistent with d(2) = 2). It describes 5x5x5 as open, which means it does not count the 2025 width-7 result as a settlement of width 5. Its general claim that m=n=k>=3 boards are draws, if right, would give d(n) at least 3 for every n at least 3; its source [7] is not identified, and MathWorld and the CRC tables say widths 6 and 7 on n x n boards are not fully analysed, so the claim is unverified.
events.doubts: Its general n x n draw claim (Section 10.4) conflicts with MathWorld and the CRC tables on widths 6 and 7, and its reference [7] is not identified. The 5x5x5 open statement is cited, not proved. I read Sections 1 to 10 in part; Section 6.12 is not in the part I read.
events.direction: Survey with a mix of cited claims; the 2x2 claim is consistent with d(2) = 2; the general n x n draw claim would cut against an X win at dimension 2 for all widths at least 3, if true.

disputes.summary: Credit for HJ(3,3) at least 22. Mouhib and Halbeisen (arXiv:2606.22155 v1 per search excerpt; reference [28] of 2607.02226) are credited by Conlon, Farnsworth and Robertson (2607.18111, Remark 9) as having proved it first. The v2 of 2606.22155 and 2607.02226 are single-author Mouhib papers; 2607.02226 says it extracts material from Mouhib's MSc thesis under Halbeisen's supervision. The record does not settle who first established the bound beyond the preprint dates.

Shelah arXiv:2607.14732. The v1 abstract (as shown on the abstract page) describes the classical Hales-Jewett numbers bounded by a tower of exponentiations, and the current abstract page calls the density version future work. The v2 text describes the density Hales-Jewett numbers bounded in E^5 and says the earlier E^4 proof is retracted. The text says E^4 in one place and E^5 in others.

Widths 6 and 7 on n x n boards. The 2026 survey (2605.20243, Section 10.4) states '(m,n,k) is a draw whenever m=n=k>=3' citing its reference [7]. MathWorld and the CRC tables say the cases n=6 and n=7 have not been fully analysed for an n x n board. The survey's reference [7] is not identified, so I cannot tell which is right.

Dates for the Qubic re-solution. Allis and Schoo 'Qubic solved again' is dated 1992 in the Wikipedia citation, 1991 in a Darse Billings note, and 1994 in NBC News. Separately, a Rochester course page says the 4x4x4 first-player win was not known until the early 1990s, which conflicts with Patashnik's 1980 publication. I treat the Rochester date as an error.

summary: The question asks for d(n), the least dimension in which the first player X has a winning strategy at width n. Known small values, as far as my sources go: d(2) = 2 (on the 2x2 board X wins in two dimensions; d = 1 is never a win for width above 1, per the Nd game article; the 2026 survey also states 2x2 is a first-player win). d(3) = 3: the 3x3 game is a draw, and the 3x3x3 game is a first-player win per Gardner 1979 as cited by MathWorld and the Wikipedia 3D article, which says it cannot end in a draw. d(4) = 3 if the 4x4 two-dimensional draw is right: Uiterwijk (arXiv 2017) claims a direct proof that the empty 4x4 board is a draw for four-in-a-row, and that is the only source I found that proves it (MathWorld gives a 5x5 draw, not 4x4); the 4x4x4 first-player win is established by Mahalko (1976, weak), Patashnik (1980) and Allis and Schoo (1992). Width 5: MathWorld, without citation, says a draw can always be obtained on 5x5 (so d(5) is at least 3), and the 2025 paper and the 2026 survey both list 5x5x5 as open. Width 6: the 2D board is not fully analysed (MathWorld and CRC), and 6x6x6 is not addressed by any source I found. Width 7: the 2025 Cain-Raymond-Källersjö result shows no first-player win at 7x7x7 under standard rules, so d(7) is at least 4; it is computer-assisted and unrefereed. Width 8 and above: at dimension 3 either player can force a draw (the 2025 paper, citing Golomb and Hales), so d(n) is at least 4 for n at least 8; MathWorld says draws can be forced in 2D for widths 8 and 9, uncited. The Hales-Jewett numbers bound d(n) from above only: by strategy stealing, if the game is not a first-player win then some balanced line-free 2-colouring exists, so d(n) is at most HJ(n,2). That is my inference; no source I read states it. On that reading the 2026 lower-bound preprints (Mouhib, 2606.22155 and 2607.02226; Conlon-Farnsworth-Robertson, 2607.18111) move nothing about d(n), because a lower bound on HJ does not bound the game from below, and the Shelah preprint (2607.14732) would give tower-type upper bounds on d(n) only if its classical reading holds, which its versions contradict. The Hindman-Tressler value HJ(3,2) = 4 (2014) gives d(3) at most 4, and Lavrov's HJ(4,2) at most 10^11 (2015) gives d(4) at most 10^11; both are weaker than the known small values. Where the call was close: (a) the 2025 width-7 result is a bound at one width, not a value, and the question asks for a function, so whether it counts as movement is for the judging pass; (b) Uiterwijk's 4x4 draw is a single abstract-level claim, and if it fails d(4) could be 2; (c) the survey's general claim that all n x n boards with n at least 3 are draws (Section 10.4) would, if true, make d(n) at least 3 for every n at least 3, but its source is unidentified and it conflicts with MathWorld on widths 6 and 7. AI involvement: none of the events credits an AI system. Searches for AI involvement (AI and LLM terms with Qubic, tic-tac-toe, the n^d game and Hales-Jewett; AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof and GPT-5 with combinatorics; lab announcements) returned no result for this problem; the AI results found in 2026 concern Ramsey numbers and other problems. The coloring preprints and the 2025 cubic paper disclose only SAT or matching computation, which is not AI. The 2026 survey (2605.20243) is the one source where an AI system appears in the same document: it credits ChatGPT with the C programs in Section 6.12 (quoted in the record) and marks some examples as AI-assisted, but I could not tell which game those programs compute, so I record it as involvement without a system in the result. Dates: all window events are first public written arguments on arXiv; I did not find journal versions of any of them.
competing_reading: The 2025 width-7 result could be read as no movement at all: the problem asks for a function d(n) of the width, and one negative case at width 7 leaves d(7) unknown above 4, so it settles only a lower bound at one point. The opposite reading treats it as a genuine restricted-case resolution, since it is the first new exact information about the first-player outcome for any width since the Qubic solution in the 1980s and 1990s. For the small values, the width-4 result depends on Uiterwijk's abstract-level 4x4 draw; if that fails, d(4) would be 2 and the small-width picture changes. For the AI question, a reader who counts proof-number search (Allis 1992) as an AI technique, since it comes from the AI literature, would record a system for the 1992 event; I have not, because it is a classical game-tree search with no learned component. The Hales-Jewett linkage is a further close call: if the judging pass holds that an upper bound on the classical 2-colour numbers bounds d(n), then Shelah's preprint and Lavrov's and Hindman-Tressler's results count as bounds on this problem; if it holds that they are about a different quantity, they count for nothing. The survey's general n x n draw claim, if the reference [7] turns out to support it, would move the lower bound for every width at least 3, and would be a much larger event than anything else in this record.
what_would_settle_it: For d(7) and the width-7 event: an independent re-run of the 2509.21494 computation (its code is linked from the arXiv HTML), a journal version, or a published first-player win at 7x7x4 or any dimension above 3 for width 7. For d(4): the full text of Uiterwijk's 4x4 direct proof and whether it was published, or Patashnik's paper read directly to confirm the strategy and the 4x4x4 result. For the width-5 and width-6 two-dimensional values: a primary source for 5x5 and 6x6 draws (MathWorld's 5x5 claim is uncited). For the survey's general n x n claim: the identity of reference [7] in arXiv:2605.20243. For the Hales-Jewett bridge: an explicit statement by Shelah or the Hales-Jewett literature that the classical numbers HJ(n,2) bound the game's winning dimension, or a clarification of which quantity the v1 abstract of 2607.14732 bounds. For the attribution dispute: the v1 text of 2606.22155 and the Mouhib-Halbeisen preprint date. For AI: the contribution statements of the coloring papers if any appear in full text beyond the portions I read (2606.22155 and 2607.02226 were read to 100,000 characters of about 193,000 and 126,000).

event.what_happened: John W. Cain, Ioannis M. Raymond and Nora C. Källersjö, 'Cubic tic-tac-toe: A matching-based approach' (arXiv:2509.21494, math.CO, v1 only, 21 pages). The paper proves, under Maker-Breaker rules, that Breaker has a winning strategy in the 7x7x7 game (Theorem 4.1), and states (Corollary 4.2) that under standard rules either player can force a draw. So X has no winning strategy on width 7, dimension 3. The method is computer-assisted: O's first four moves (or three, depending on X's opening) are fixed so that the remaining play follows a pairing found as a maximal matching in a bipartite graph, computed with Hopcroft-Karp. It checks 22,163,142 configurations after an opening at the centre (matchings of size 332 over 166 surviving lines) and 12,824,370 otherwise (matchings of size 336 over 168 lines). The introduction states the known results: the first player wins for n at most 4 (citing Patashnik), either player forces a draw for n at least 8 (citing Golomb and Hales), and widths 5 and 6 are open.
event.revisions: v1 25 Sep 2025 only; no later version listed on the abstract page when fetched
event.delivers: Width 7 at dimension 3 only: no first-player winning strategy under standard rules, so d(7) is at least 4. It establishes nothing about widths 5 and 6 at dimension 3, nothing about whether X wins at width 7 in dimension 4 or above, and nothing about any other width. It is a restricted case of the question: one width, one dimension, and the claim is a negative one about X.
event.remains: Width 5 and width 6 at dimension 3 (open per the paper). Width 7 at every dimension of 4 or more, so d(7) is known only to be at least 4. Widths 5 and 6 at dimension 2 are not addressed by this paper (see the survey and MathWorld for claims there).
event.directly_checkable: The proof is a finite computation whose output is explicit: for each listed configuration, a perfect matching of the stated size gives Breaker's answers. The authors say their code and compilation instructions are at people.math.harvard.edu/~jcain2/tic-tac-toe-code.tar.gz (linked from the arXiv HTML). I did not download or run it.
event.doubts: No public check found. It is unrefereed (no journal reference), computer-assisted, and the code had not been re-run by anyone I could find. The paper's statements about widths 4 and at least 8 are cited to Patashnik and Golomb-Hales in the body, which I read only in part. No specific error has been identified.
event.direction: Cuts against a first-player win at width 7 in dimension 3, so the least winning dimension for width 7 exceeds 3.
event.object: A computer-verified pairing strategy for the second player on the 7x7x7 board: after four opening moves for each side (three if X does not open at the centre), the surviving lines admit a perfect matching (size 332 or 336) that tells O how to answer, and the paper checks all such configurations. It shows that X cannot force a win in dimension 3 at width 7. It is explicit as a finite certificate, not a non-constructive existence argument.

ai.disclosed_cost: about five hours of computation on the first author's laptop, per the paper

events.credibility_reason: Known only from a Wikipedia citation; no catalogue record or text found.

v2 retracts the v1 proof, switches the object to density HJ numbers, is internally inconsistent (E^4 vs E^5) and defers the main argument to a future full version; the bearing on d(n) is the researcher's inference.
Survey whose general n x n draw claim rests on an unidentified reference and conflicts with MathWorld.

judgement.why: The statement asks for the least winning dimension d(n) as a function of the width. Cain-Raymond-Källersjö show 7x7x7 is not a first-player win, so d(7) >= 4: that moves a lower bound at one width without fixing d(7), so it is a bound, not a case. I marked it checkable because it is an explicit finite matching certificate with public code, and it uses no AI (Hopcroft-Karp matching). The Mouhib and Conlon-Farnsworth-Robertson preprints give lower bounds on Hales-Jewett colouring numbers, and those bound nothing about the game from below, so they are variants. Bastioni et al. play a different game, so also a variant. Shelah's upper bound on HJ numbers would cap d(n) from above, so I kept it as a bound, but marked it doubtful because of the retraction and version confusion. Before the snapshot, Patashnik 1980 (journal paper plus Thompson's check) settles the first-player win at width 4, dimension 3; with Uiterwijk's 4x4 draw that pins d(4) = 3, so I scored it as a case. No pre-snapshot event settles the whole function.
judgement.doubts: Close call between scoring Cain et al. as a case (it settles the X-wins question at width 7, dimension 3) and as a bound (it leaves d(7) undetermined); I chose bound because the statement asks for the value of d(n). Whether Shelah v2 still bounds the classical numbers, and so d(n), is unclear from the record. In the survey, ChatGPT is credited with C programs, but no system is listed in ai.systems and the survey proves nothing, so it gets none.
judgement.by: judging pass (JUDGE.md), claude-opus-5-5; not the researching agent and not a human reviewer
